rationale: A wins because it is more disciplined: three real angles, three different desks, and fewer facts smuggled in wearing a trench coat. A's best line, "Monzo returns to the US — this time renting a banking license instead of chasing one," is sharp and grounded in the partner-bank versus license shift. B has good instincts, but "Nine million UK customers, zero in the US" invents a clean contrast the update does not give, and "road to IPO" wanders in from another pitch deck.
gaps_in_A: "Monzo posted its first annual profit — then spent it on a second shot at America" overstates causality. The update gives sequence, not that profit funded the US move.
"A 9-million-customer UK bank tests whether its home playbook survives America" is directionally good, but "home playbook" needs product specifics the update does not provide.
"Any same-day news-peg angle" is a muddy refusal. The launch itself is a same-day peg; the real point is that no external breaking peg was supplied.
gaps_in_B: "Nine million UK customers, zero in the US" is invented. The update says invite-only launch, not zero US customers or no beta users.
"road to IPO" is unsupported. No IPO fact, plan, banker chatter, or timing appears in the update.
"then immediately spent it on the market that beat it once" repeats the same funding-causality overreach: profit and launch are sequenced, not linked.

"Monzo is launching a US bank account it won't let most people open" may work as a consumer hook, but it turns "invite-only at first" into a broader access claim without invite volume or eligibility facts.
